title: B2B Ecommerce Development Partner Selection: A Buyer's Guide
summary: A practical B2B ecommerce development partner selection guide: evaluation criteria, real cost ranges, a weighted scoring matrix, and APAC platform fit.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Start by choosing an operating model — project agency, systems integrator, or managed squad — then score shortlisted partners on B2B domain experience, ERP depth, team continuity, and exit terms. Validate the top candidate with a paid two-sprint pilot before signing any long-term contract.


---


Gartner has projected that 80% of B2B sales interactions between suppliers and buyers will occur in digital channels by 2025 — and McKinsey's B2B Pulse research has repeatedly found that e-commerce now rivals or beats in-person selling as the most effective channel for B2B revenue. Those two numbers explain why B2B ecommerce development partner selection has become a board-level procurement decision rather than an IT line item. The partner you pick does not just build a catalogue. They determine how your dealer network places repeat orders, how your ERP pricing logic gets enforced, and how fast you can open a second country.

*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus vs Adobe Ecommerce Stock: An APAC Operator's View](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-vs-adobe-ecommerce-stock-apac-decision)


*Related reading:*[LLM Hallucination Risk in APAC Workflows: A Procurement Guide](https://branch8.com/posts/llm-hallucination-risk-apac-workflows-procurement)


I have spent the last decade building commerce systems for listed retail groups, multi-brand catering operators, and manufacturers selling through dealer networks across Greater China and Southeast Asia. The pattern I see most often is not a bad build. It is a correct build delivered by a partner who had no plan for month 13 — the point at which the project team disbands, the agency rotates staff, and the client is left owning a codebase nobody on their payroll understands.


This guide is written to help you avoid that. It covers the evaluation criteria that actually predict outcomes, honest cost ranges, a weighted scoring framework you can run on a shortlist, and the structural difference between hiring a project agency and standing up a managed squad.


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus Enterprise Fit & Cost Comparison for APAC Brands](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-enterprise-fit-cost-comparison-apac)


## You are not choosing a builder, you are choosing an operating model


Most partner selection processes start with the wrong question: "who can build this?" Plenty of firms can. The sharper question is "who will still be improving this in 24 months, and at what cost per unit of change?"


B2B commerce is not a launch-and-leave asset. Unlike a D2C storefront where the merchandising team can self-serve most changes, B2B platforms carry continuous engineering load:


- Customer-specific price lists and contract pricing that change quarterly
- Approval workflows, purchase order rules, and credit limits tied to the ERP
- New dealer or distributor onboarding, each with its own tax, currency, and shipping rules
- Punchout and EDI integrations for buyers whose procurement systems dictate the format
- Quote-to-order flows that mirror how your sales reps actually negotiate


A listed Greater China jewellery retailer we worked with illustrated the shape of the problem well: the wholesale side of the business needed per-account pricing tiers that changed with metal costs, while the retail side needed fast campaign merchandising. Those are two different engineering cadences on one platform. A fixed-scope project contract cannot absorb that. A standing team can.


So before you evaluate vendors, decide which operating model you are buying:


**Project agency.** Fixed scope, fixed-ish price, defined end date. Good for a first build with clear requirements. Weak when requirements evolve mid-flight, and the handover cliff is real.


**Systems integrator.** Large, process-heavy, strong on ERP and compliance. Appropriate above roughly USD 1M of programme spend. Expensive per unit of change and slow to turn around small requests.


**Managed squad / staff augmentation.** A dedicated, named team working on a monthly retainer against a rolling backlog, embedded in your tooling and reporting to your product owner. Continuity is the product. Trade-off: you need internal capacity to prioritise, or you will pay for a team that waits for decisions.


*Related reading:*[Salesforce CRM OAuth Security Incident Response: APAC Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-crm-oauth-security-incident-response-apac-playbook)


**In-house build.** Maximum control, slowest to start. In Hong Kong, Singapore, and Sydney, senior commerce engineers are among the hardest roles to fill; the hiring lag alone often exceeds the time to launch with a partner.


Branch8 runs the managed squad model because it matches how B2B commerce actually consumes engineering. I will be direct about the trade-off: if you genuinely have a one-off build with frozen requirements and no roadmap after launch, a fixed-price agency is cheaper. Most B2B programmes are not that.


## Eleven evaluation criteria that predict outcomes


The top-ranking advice on this topic tends to stop at "check their certifications" and "look at their partner network." Certifications are table stakes. Here is what actually separates partners once the contract is signed.


### 1. B2B-specific commerce experience, not B2C volume


Ask for two references where the partner implemented contract pricing, multi-tier account hierarchies, or quote-to-order. A thousand Shopify storefronts does not mean they have modelled a parent-child account structure with buyer-level permissions. The platform skills overlap; the domain modelling does not.


### 2. ERP and middleware depth


B2B commerce is, functionally, a presentation layer over your ERP's pricing and inventory truth. Ask which ERPs they have integrated — SAP, Dynamics 365 Business Central, NetSuite, Odoo, or regional systems like Wingsang and Tally — and whether they wrote the middleware or bought a connector. Then ask what happens when the ERP is down. A partner who cannot describe their caching and retry strategy has not been through a real go-live.


### 3. Named team continuity


Get the names and the commitment in writing. Many agencies pitch with principals and deliver with juniors. The question I would ask: "Which of the people in this room will be in sprint review in month nine, and what is your bench rotation policy?"


### 4. Time zone and language overlap with your operations


If your warehouse is in Shenzhen, your finance team in Singapore, and your dealers in Jakarta and Manila, a partner working US Eastern hours gives you a two-hour daily overlap. For APAC-headquartered brands and for US or EU companies running Asian supply chains, a partner based in the region turns support from next-day to same-hour. This is the single most underweighted criterion in most RFPs.


### 5. Code ownership and exit terms


The contract should state plainly that you own the repository, the infrastructure accounts, and the documentation. Ask for the offboarding clause before you ask for the price. A partner who has a clean, rehearsed answer here is a partner who has done it without drama.


### 6. Architecture opinion — and the reasoning behind it


Any partner who recommends a platform before understanding your order volume, SKU count, pricing complexity, and integration surface is selling what they have, not what you need. Push them: "Under what conditions would you advise against the platform you just recommended?" The quality of the negative case tells you more than the pitch.


### 7. Delivery cadence and observable progress


Two-week sprints with a working demo environment beat monthly status decks. Ask to see a real sprint board from a live engagement (redacted). If they cannot produce one, delivery discipline is aspirational.


### 8. QA and release engineering


Ask how they deploy. If the answer is manual FTP or a single production branch, the cost of every future change goes up. You want to hear about CI pipelines, staging parity, and automated regression on checkout and pricing. For example, a minimally serious Shopify theme deployment looks like this:


```text
1  # Shopify CLI — themed deploys gated by environment    2  shopify theme push --environment staging --json    3  shopify theme check --fail-level error    4  # Promote only after regression suite passes    5  shopify theme push --environment production --allow-live
```


And on Adobe Commerce, a partner should be running something close to:


```text
1  bin/magento setup:upgrade --keep-generated    2  bin/magento setup:di:compile    3  bin/magento setup:static-content:deploy en_US zh_Hant --jobs 4    4  bin/magento indexer:reindex catalog_product_price    5  bin/magento cache:flush
```


If those commands are unfamiliar to the people in the room, you are talking to salespeople, not engineers.


### 9. Multi-country and multi-currency readiness


For APAC expansion you will need per-market catalogues, local payment methods (PayMe and FPS in Hong Kong, PayNow in Singapore, QRIS in Indonesia, GrabPay across the region), and tax handling that survives Australian GST, Singapore GST, and Malaysian SST. Ask for a market they launched that was not the home market.


### 10. Data and privacy compliance posture


If you handle buyer data across jurisdictions, your partner needs working familiarity with Hong Kong's PDPO, Singapore's PDPA, Australia's Privacy Act, and — if you sell into Europe — GDPR. Mainland China's PIPL adds cross-border transfer obligations that catch a lot of teams out.


### 11. Commercial flexibility


Can they scale a squad from two to five engineers for a peak season and back down again? Fixed-scope contracts cannot. This matters more than headline rate for anyone with seasonal demand.

## Platform fit: Shopify Plus, Adobe Commerce, SHOPLINE, BigCommerce


Partner selection and platform selection are entangled, because most partners are specialists. Evaluate the platform honestly first, then shortlist partners who are strong on it.


### Shopify Plus


Shopify's B2B functionality — company profiles, price lists, payment terms, and B2B-specific checkout — is now native to Plus rather than requiring a separate wholesale channel. Strengths: fastest time to launch, low operational overhead, excellent for brands running B2B and D2C side by side. Constraints: deeply custom pricing logic and complex approval chains often push you into app stacking or headless with Hydrogen, which erodes the simplicity advantage. Shopify publishes Plus pricing from USD 2,300 per month on an annual contract.


### Adobe Commerce


The B2B module set — requisition lists, company accounts, negotiable quotes, shared catalogues — is the most complete out of the box. Adobe's own documentation is extensive and its developer tooling (App Builder, API Mesh) is mature. Constraints: total cost of ownership is high, the license is quoted per GMV band, and you need a partner with genuine Adobe Commerce engineering depth rather than a front-end shop.


### SHOPLINE


Strong in Greater China and Southeast Asia, with payment, logistics, and social commerce integrations tuned for the region — WhatsApp and LINE flows, local carriers, and cross-border settlement. For an APAC-first B2B brand whose buyers transact over messaging apps before they ever see a portal, this regional fit is substantive. Constraints: a smaller global developer pool and less mature B2B account hierarchy than Adobe.


### BigCommerce


Open SaaS with a usable B2B Edition and generous API limits. A reasonable middle path between Shopify's simplicity and Adobe's depth. Smaller partner bench in APAC than in North America.


The honest heuristic: if your pricing rules fit in a spreadsheet and your orders are repeat-heavy, Shopify Plus or BigCommerce will serve you. If your pricing rules require a decision tree and your buyers run procurement systems, Adobe Commerce earns its cost. If your growth is regional and messaging-led, SHOPLINE deserves a real evaluation rather than a dismissal.


## What B2B ecommerce development actually costs


The sector is coy about numbers, so here are observed market ranges as of late 2025. These are industry rate bands, not quotes.


### Platform licensing (annual)


- **Shopify Plus:** from USD 2,300/month on an annual term, per Shopify's published pricing; variable fees apply above certain GMV.
- **Adobe Commerce:** license commonly quoted in the USD 22,000–125,000+ per year range depending on GMV band and whether you take Adobe Commerce on Cloud. Hosting on Cloud is bundled; self-managed infrastructure adds AWS or GCP spend.
- **BigCommerce Enterprise:** typically quoted in the low-to-mid five figures annually, GMV-banded.
- **SHOPLINE:** regionally priced, generally the lowest licence tier of the four, with transaction-based components.


### Implementation


- **Mid-market B2B build (single market, one ERP integration, 1,000–20,000 SKUs):** USD 60,000–200,000.
- **Enterprise B2B build (multi-market, multi-ERP, punchout/EDI, custom pricing engine):** USD 250,000–1,000,000+.
- **Replatform from a legacy portal:** add 20–40% for data migration and reconciliation, which is almost always underestimated. Order history, credit terms, and account hierarchies rarely map cleanly.


### Engineering rates by region


- **US / UK / Western Europe senior commerce engineer:** USD 150–250 per hour through an agency.
- **Australia / New Zealand:** AUD 180–260 per hour.
- **Hong Kong / Singapore:** USD 80–140 per hour.
- **Vietnam / Philippines / Malaysia delivery centres:** USD 35–70 per hour.


The arbitrage is real, and it is why a growing number of US and EU brands now run their commerce engineering from an APAC hub. But raw rate is the wrong unit. A USD 45/hour engineer who needs three iterations to ship a pricing rule is more expensive than a USD 110/hour engineer who ships it once. Compare cost per shipped increment, not cost per hour.


### Managed squad retainers


A dedicated two-to-four person squad (engineer, senior engineer, QA, fractional tech lead) sourced through an APAC partner typically lands in the USD 8,000–30,000 per month band depending on seniority mix and location. Against the all-in cost of hiring equivalent staff in Hong Kong or Singapore — where Robert Half and Michael Page salary guides consistently place senior full-stack engineers above HKD 60,000 per month before on-costs — the retainer usually prices below a two-person in-house team, with no recruitment lag and no single-point-of-failure risk.


### Ongoing run costs people forget


Budget 15–25% of initial build cost annually for maintenance, platform version upgrades, security patching, and integration drift. Adobe Commerce upgrades in particular are non-trivial engineering events, not maintenance windows.

## Score your shortlist with a weighted decision matrix


Run this on three to five vendors. Score each criterion 1–5, multiply by the weight, and sum. A maximum score is 500.


### The weights


- **B2B domain experience — weight 15.** Contract pricing, account hierarchies, quote-to-order shipped at least twice.
- **ERP / integration depth — weight 15.** Named ERPs, written middleware, documented failure handling.
- **Team continuity — weight 12.** Named individuals, retention data, bench policy.
- **Platform engineering depth — weight 12.** Can demonstrate code, not just screenshots.
- **Time zone and regional coverage — weight 10.** Overlap with your operations and your markets.
- **Delivery discipline — weight 10.** Sprint cadence, demo environments, visible backlog.
- **Commercial flexibility — weight 8.** Can scale up and down; no change-order tax on small requests.
- **Code ownership and exit terms — weight 8.** Clean offboarding clause, you own everything.
- **Compliance posture — weight 5.** PDPO, PDPA, GDPR, PIPL as applicable.
- **Cultural and communication fit — weight 5.** Does your product owner want to be in a room with them weekly?


### How to read the result


- **400+:** Strong fit. Proceed to a paid discovery or a two-sprint pilot.
- **320–399:** Viable with named gaps. Write the gaps into the contract as obligations.
- **Below 320:** Do not proceed on price alone. Low scores on continuity and ERP depth are the ones that bite in month 13.


Two refinements worth applying. First, make B2B domain experience and ERP depth *gating* criteria — a score of 1 or 2 on either disqualifies regardless of total. Second, weight the time-zone criterion higher if you are a European or North American business running Asian manufacturing or distribution; overlap with your supply chain often matters more than overlap with your head office.


## Build a selection form that filters before the sales call


The fastest way to compress a partner selection process is to send a structured questionnaire before any demo. Ten questions, written answers, 48-hour turnaround. It filters out firms that cannot answer without a pre-sales engineer.


1. Name three B2B commerce implementations with contract pricing. Which ERP, which platform, which year?
2. Who specifically would staff this engagement, and what is their current allocation?
3. Describe your deployment pipeline from commit to production.
4. How do you handle an ERP outage during checkout?
5. What is your average engineer tenure?
6. Which platform would you recommend here, and under what conditions would you advise against it?
7. What are your offboarding terms and who owns the repository?
8. Which non-home markets have you launched, with which payment methods?
9. How do you price a 20-hour change request mid-engagement?
10. What did you get wrong on your last B2B project, and what changed as a result?


Question 10 is the one that matters. Anyone who claims nothing went wrong has either not delivered a complex B2B build or is not going to tell you the truth when yours goes sideways.

## Red flags worth walking away from


- **Fixed price for an undefined scope.** Either they will pad it heavily or they will absorb the loss by cutting quality. Both are your problem.
- **No staging environment in the proposal.** Means testing happens in production.
- **Pitch team ≠ delivery team,** with no named handover.
- **Platform recommendation before discovery.** They are selling inventory.
- **Reluctance to discuss exit.** The partners who have handed over cleanly will tell you about it; those who lock clients in change the subject.
- **No regional presence for a regional rollout.** Launching Indonesia or Vietnam from a Western time zone with no local payment or logistics relationships is a multi-month tax.


## How to evaluate: a sequence that works


Run the process in this order, and resist the urge to compress it.


**Weeks 1–2: define the operating model.** Decide whether you are buying a project, an integrator programme, or a standing squad. Write down your roadmap for months 13–24. If that roadmap is substantial, weight continuity accordingly in your B2B ecommerce development partner selection.


**Week 3: send the ten-question form** to six to eight candidates. Expect two or three to self-select out.


**Weeks 4–5: score the shortlist** against the weighted matrix with at least three internal stakeholders scoring independently — commercial, IT, and operations. Reconcile the variance; disagreement usually reveals an unstated requirement.


**Week 6: run a paid discovery or a two-sprint pilot** with your top one or two. Pay for it. A paid pilot on a real backlog item — a pricing rule, an ERP sync, a quote flow — tells you more than any reference call. You are buying evidence of how they work, not a deliverable.


**Week 7: negotiate on structure, not rate.** Lock named staffing, sprint cadence, code ownership, and offboarding. Rate is the easiest term to agree and the least predictive of outcome.


Where is this heading? Two forces are reshaping partner selection in APAC. The first is composable architecture becoming cheaper to adopt — API-first catalogue, pricing, and checkout services mean partners are increasingly judged on integration judgement rather than platform certifications. The second is AI-assisted engineering compressing the cost of routine build work while raising the premium on the people who can model a complicated pricing domain correctly in the first place. Both push value away from headcount and towards continuity and domain depth. The partners who win the next cycle will be the ones who can hold your commerce logic in their heads for three years, not the ones who can build your catalogue in three months.


If you are mapping a B2B commerce roadmap across Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, or Australia — or running an APAC build from a US or European head office — Branch8 can walk through the squad model and where it does and does not fit your situation. Bring your month-13 roadmap to the conversation; that is the document that decides the answer.
